title: A Plea from the Falsely Accused
overview: Someone wrongly accused asks God, pictured as the judge of all the world, to see his innocence, stop his attackers, and let their schemes backfire.

parts.label: Running to God for safety (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The speaker flees to God as to a shelter, afraid his pursuers will maul him like a lion with no one to stop them. The heading links the psalm to David and a man named Cush from Saul's tribe, but who Cush was is unknown.

parts.label: An oath of innocence (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: He swears that if he betrayed a friend, his attacker may trample him into the dust, a serious way to deny a specific charge rather than a claim to be perfect. The Hebrew of verse 4 is unclear: some translations have him deny robbing an enemy, while others have him say he actually spared one, which may recall David sparing Saul's life.

parts.label: Calling the judge to court (vv. 6-9)
parts.note: God is pictured as a judge who seems asleep, asked to wake, take his high seat, and rule with the nations gathered around. The speaker asks to be cleared by the God who sees into people's hidden thoughts and motives.

parts.label: God as armed defender (vv. 10-13)
parts.note: God shields the honest but is also shown as a warrior sharpening a sword and readying flaming arrows against those who do harm. The weapons picture God's readiness to act against wrongdoing, though verse 12 is worded differently across translations.

parts.label: Evil comes back around (vv. 14-16)
parts.note: Plotting harm is pictured as a pregnancy that ends in nothing but disappointment. The person who digs a trap for others falls into it, and their violence lands on their own head.

parts.label: A closing song of thanks (v. 17)
parts.note: The speaker ends by thanking the LORD for being fair. The psalm moves from fear to confidence that justice will win out.

disagreement: Readers differ on verse 12: some take it to mean God holds back judgment if a wrongdoer turns around, leaving room for change, while others read it as God simply not relenting from judgment.
think: When someone has wronged you, where is the line between wanting justice and wanting them to suffer?
